title: the mountain ahead
hookLine: the mountain ahead; the prayers Jesus himself prayed
last: TALK TO HIM LIKE A FRIEND.

cards: Look back down the hill for a second. Three weeks ago you started with the sign of the cross. Then the Eucharist.
Mary. The Hail Mary. The Our Father.

teach.b: The Psalms are a book of one hundred and fifty songs and prayers in the middle of the Bible. The Hebrew name is Tehillim: praises. Our word psalm comes from Greek, a song sung to a plucked string.
They were Israel's prayer book and hymnal, and Jesus, a Jewish boy in Nazareth, likely grew up hearing them. Here's what surprises people: they aren't all nice. Some are joyful.
Some are furious. Some are people in the dark asking God where he's gone.

teach.h: MY GOD, WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME?
teach.b: On the cross, in Matthew's Gospel, Jesus cries out the first line of one of those, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" That's a psalm.
In that hour, he prays in words that were already old. And in another Gospel, his last words are from a psalm too: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit."

teach.h: THE NUMBERS ARE OFF BY ONE.
teach.b: One detail, if you ever look them up in an older Catholic Bible: the numbers are often off by one.
The Douay-Rheims follows the ancient Greek and Latin count, so the psalm Jesus cried on the cross is Psalm 21 there, and Psalm 22 in Bibles that follow the Hebrew. Same words, different count.
The Church still prays them every day. At every Mass there's a psalm between the readings, the one from day twelve, sung back and forth.
Priests, monks and nuns pray the psalms through the day in what's called the Liturgy of the Hours. And the rosary from day four, the poor man's psalter, grew up in their shadow.
One hundred and fifty psalms, one for nearly every feeling a person can have.

how: At every Mass a psalm is sung or said between the readings, and priests, religious and many lay Catholics pray the psalms through the day in the Liturgy of the Hours.

practice: Here's the practice for the end of camp one. Ask yourself what you're actually feeling today, honestly. Glad.
Grateful. Whatever it is, the Psalms have a door for it, and you don't have to clean it up first. Name the feeling in one word.
Then breathe with it, not against it. If you pray, you can hand God that one word, just as it is.
